final_idea.title: Does attendance burden modify the benefit of a post-G1 tutoring offer?
final_idea.question: Among secondary students eligible for support after the first grading period, does a randomized offer of structured subject tutoring improve second-period grade change more for students with higher absence counts measured strictly before G1 than for students with lower counts?
final_idea.new_claim: The proposed increment is a decision-specific effect-modification question: a dated pre-G1 attendance measure may help determine whether tutoring offers should be prioritized by attendance burden, beyond predicting grades. This is an untested hypothesis, not a finding.
final_idea.input_delta: Adds a defined post-G1 support decision, a temporally prior absence measure and a randomized-offer-by-absence contrast. The supplied material describes grade prediction and observational support but does not establish this intervention question.
final_idea.domain_value: Could guide whether schools should prioritize tutoring outreach for students with greater pre-period absence burden, if a randomized trial demonstrates a useful differential benefit.
known_basis_refs: input: official documentation defines G1 and G2 as first- and second-period grades on a 0-20 scale and schoolsup as extra educational support, without timing or assignment details
input: 649 student records from two Portuguese schools; absences are a count with no stated observation window
tool:c1: schoolsup-by-absences>=3 adjusted descriptive interaction 0.678 grade points, HC3 SE 0.486, normal 95% interval [-0.275, 1.631], N=649, design rank 9/9
assumptions: A prospective protocol can measure absence days strictly before G1 and record tutoring offer, uptake and dose.
Random assignment of the offer is ethical among eligible students; if not, a defensible randomized encouragement is required and the estimand must be changed accordingly.
G1 and G2 are dated and comparable 0-20 subject-grade measurements, with G2 recorded after the offer.
final_idea.variables_and_units: Student is the assignment and analysis unit. Record pre-G1 absence days over a fixed stated window (days), G1 and G2 grades (grade points, 0-20), randomized tutoring offer (0/1), uptake and attended sessions (sessions), school and subject. Primary outcome is G2-G1 in grade points. Pre-register a high-absence threshold with educators before enrollment; retain the continuous absence-by-offer interaction as a secondary analysis. The primary estimand is the difference between offer effects across the pre-specified absence strata under intention-to-treat.
final_idea.testable_prediction: The supplied-data proxy estimate is positive (0.678 grade points) in the predicted direction, but uncertain: its 95% interval [-0.275, 1.631] includes zero. This does not test the intervention claim. Proposal-only randomized prediction: the offer effect on G2-G1 is larger in the pre-specified high-absence stratum. No effect size is established.
final_idea.alternative: Absence burden may mark barriers that reduce tutoring uptake, so the offer effect could be smaller among students with higher absence counts; alternatively, schools may have targeted existing support to students with greater unmeasured need, distorting the observational proxy in either direction.
final_idea.discriminating_test: Run a pre-registered student-level randomized offer after G1, stratified by a threshold on absence days measured before G1. Compare assigned offer versus control on G2-G1 by stratum using intention-to-treat, and report the offer-by-absence interaction and interval. Record uptake to describe implementation without replacing the assignment estimand. Set a practically useful interaction threshold with school stakeholders before enrollment; support attendance-based prioritization only if the interval's lower bound exceeds that threshold. Otherwise reject that allocation rule, while estimating any overall offer effect separately.
final_idea.feasible_with_current_data: Only a descriptive proxy contrast is feasible. The supplied absences have no stated time window, schoolsup has no stated timing or dose, and support is not randomized. The randomized effect-modification question cannot be tested in these data.
final_idea.required_new_data: Prospective trial or randomized encouragement with student-level assignment; fixed-window timestamped absence days before G1; eligibility and randomization records; dated G1 and G2 subject grades; tutoring offer, uptake and session count; school and subject identifiers; and a stakeholder-defined minimum useful interaction threshold with an adequate power calculation.
final_idea.failure_condition: For the proposal, the allocation hypothesis fails if a sufficiently powered pre-registered trial does not show a positive offer-by-absence interaction whose confidence interval lower bound exceeds the predeclared useful-benefit threshold. A null or negative result rejects attendance-based prioritization, though it does not by itself rule out an overall tutoring benefit.
final_idea.nearest_prior_query: Search randomized or encouragement-based secondary-school tutoring studies that test baseline absenteeism as a moderator of subsequent grade effects, distinguishing such moderation from observational support allocation and grade prediction.

original_final.what_changed: The original question is retained but tightened: the absence window must end before G1, the follow-up is a randomized offer after G1, and an educator-defined practical interaction threshold is required for the allocation decision. The unadjusted hypothesis remains proposal-only; the computed quantity is only a descriptive association using proxies.
original_final.what_is_known: The executed calculation used 649 rows. Cell counts were absences <3/support no=322, absences <3/support yes=44, absences >=3/support no=259, and absences >=3/support yes=24. The adjusted interaction was 0.678 grade points, HC3 SE 0.486, normal-approximation 95% interval [-0.275, 1.631], with full design rank 9/9. The estimate is directionally consistent with the frozen descriptive prediction but does not distinguish it from zero at this interval level. Timing and confounding prevent a causal interpretation.
original_final.what_is_new_hypothesis: Relative to the supplied prediction-focused documentation, the added hypothesis is that pre-G1 absence burden modifies the causal effect of a post-G1 tutoring offer on G2-G1 and could support a targeted allocation rule. The supplied data and search results do not establish this hypothesis or its novelty in world literature.
original_final.falsifier: A sufficiently powered randomized trial in which the pre-registered offer-by-absence interaction's interval does not exceed the stakeholder-defined minimum useful benefit falsifies the proposed attendance-based prioritization rule. A sufficiently precise non-positive interaction is especially contrary to the directional prediction.
original_final.minimum_next_test: Specify a fixed pre-G1 attendance window and eligibility rule; obtain educator agreement on the minimum useful interaction; calculate trial power; then randomize the tutoring offer within absence strata and measure dated G1, offer/uptake, and G2. Report intention-to-treat stratum effects and the interaction with uncertainty.

final_idea.title: Separate attendance-access support from tutoring at the first-period decision point
final_idea.question: Among Portuguese-course students below a school-predeclared G1 threshold at the end of period 1, does an equal-scheduled-contact attendance-access and missed-lesson recovery offer improve period-2 G2 more than subject tutoring, and is that package contrast larger in a predeclared high-absence stratum?
final_idea.new_claim: Support allocation may improve when the added-support package is matched to an attendance-access bottleneck rather than assuming all low G1 reflects subject-mastery difficulty. This is a falsifiable proposal, not a finding in the supplied records.
final_idea.input_delta: The input contains G1/G2, total absence count, coarse travel-time categories and support indicators, but no dated lesson attendance, instructional exposure, support assignment, fidelity or randomized comparison. The increment is an equal-contact randomized package contrast with a predeclared baseline-absence interaction.
final_idea.domain_value: If the package contrast is meaningfully larger for students with high baseline absence, schools could allocate added support by an actionable risk stratum; if not, a common tutoring route may be preferable. Standard or required support remains available in both arms.

case.workflow: support allocation beyond final-grade prediction
case.unit: two Portuguese schools; support not randomized; limited survey timing metadata

assumptions: The school defines an academically meaningful G1 eligibility threshold and high-absence rule before enrollment; exploratory thresholds are not school policy.
Both added-support offers can have equal scheduled contact minutes, consistent delivery and supplement standard support.
Randomization is feasible within school and risk strata, and classrooms/students support classroom-aware inference.
G2 is scored comparably across arms and aligned with material taught during the intervention.
final_idea.variables_and_units: Eligibility: G1 below a predeclared threshold (grade points, 0-20). Moderator: period-1 scheduled Portuguese lessons missed (count), grouped by a predeclared rule. Assigned offer: access-and-catch-up versus subject tutoring (categorical), with equal scheduled contact minutes per student. Proximal outcome: period-2 attended scheduled Portuguese lessons (count and proportion); primary outcome: G2 grade points (0-20). Unit: student; account for classroom/teacher clustering.
final_idea.testable_prediction: The intention-to-treat G2 contrast (access-and-catch-up minus tutoring, estimated with baseline G1 adjustment) will be positive and larger in the predeclared high-absence stratum than in the low-absence stratum. The access package is also predicted to increase period-2 attendance more than tutoring among high-absence students. Attendance improvement without a meaningful G2 advantage does not support the academic-support claim.
final_idea.alternative: Subject-mastery difficulty or general contact/attention is the main bottleneck, so tutoring matches or exceeds access-and-catch-up on G2 and the package contrast does not increase with baseline absence. Any attendance difference may fail to translate into learning.
final_idea.discriminating_test: Preregister an individually randomized, equal-scheduled-contact comparison among eligible students at period-1 end, stratified by school and predeclared absence group. Keep normal support available in both arms. Record baseline G1 and dated scheduled/attended lessons, assignment, actual package components and minutes, G2, and class/teacher. Estimate intention-to-treat G2 by ANCOVA adjusting for G1, the treatment-by-absence interaction, and attendance contrasts with classroom-aware uncertainty. Set the minimum meaningful G2 difference, missing-data rule and analysis before enrollment. Treat attendance as a proximal outcome; this comparison alone does not identify mediation.
final_idea.feasible_with_current_data: Only exploratory recruitment and descriptive summaries are possible. Existing observational support comparisons cannot estimate causal support effects, attendance response, mediation or prospective outcomes.
final_idea.required_new_data: Prospective eligibility and baseline G1; predeclared school threshold and absence rule; dated scheduled and attended Portuguese lessons in both periods; randomized offer and stratum; intervention components, fidelity and delivered minutes; G2; class/teacher identifiers; and a preregistered minimum meaningful difference and analysis plan.
final_idea.failure_condition: With adequate precision, reject the routing prediction if the high-absence stratum shows no meaningful G2 advantage for access-and-catch-up over equal-contact tutoring, or if its predicted attendance advantage is absent. If attendance improves but G2 does not, reject the stronger academic-support claim.
final_idea.nearest_prior_query: Search for secondary-school randomized or quasi-randomized comparisons of attendance/access or missed-instruction recovery support against equal-contact subject tutoring, with baseline-absence moderation, dated attendance and course-grade outcomes.

original_final.what_changed: R1 revised the candidate from an attendance-mediation framing to a randomized package-comparison question with attendance as a proximal outcome. It fixed baseline absence as the primary moderator, moved travel time to context, made baseline-adjusted G2 the primary outcome, and required equal scheduled contact plus fidelity/delivered-dose measurement. The feasibility computation informs subgroup recruitment only; the candidate's intervention prediction remains untested.
original_final.what_is_known: The supplied documentation describes 649 complete student records from two Portuguese schools, with G1/G2 and total absences but no randomized support assignment, dated attendance or reliable intervention timing. The executed descriptive calculation used provisional G1<10 and absences>=6: 157 records met G1<10. For high-absence eligible students, travel-category counts were 28, 17, 3 and 2; for lower-absence eligible students, counts were 43, 43, 18 and 3. The resulting G2-G1 summaries are observational descriptions, not support effects; sparse long-travel cells make travel-time stratification unsuitable as a primary test. Crossref returned eight mixed-relevance records. Two abstracts covered twin-study grade/attendance assumptions and an after-school reading tutoring project; several other hits were title/metadata only, including attendance and supplementary-instruction titles. None verifies the exact proposed package comparison, and the relevance-ordered search is not exhaustive.
original_final.what_is_new_hypothesis: A predeclared high baseline-absence group may benefit more on period-2 Portuguese grade from attendance-access and missed-lesson recovery support than from equal-scheduled-contact subject tutoring, with a corresponding period-2 attendance advantage. This proposal adds a decision-focused randomized package contrast and moderator beyond the supplied descriptive dataset; no world-literature novelty is established.
original_final.falsifier: In an adequately powered preregistered trial, the proposal fails if access-and-catch-up does not exceed equal-contact tutoring by the prespecified meaningful G2 amount in the high-absence stratum or if its predicted attendance advantage is absent. If attendance improves but G2 does not, the claim that access recovery is the more useful academic support fails.
original_final.minimum_next_test: In a prospective cohort of students eligible under a school-predeclared G1 threshold, randomize the access-and-catch-up versus tutoring offer within school and baseline-absence strata while retaining standard support. Record dated scheduled and attended Portuguese lessons, baseline G1, assignment, intervention components/fidelity/actual minutes, G2 and class/teacher identifiers. Preregister the minimum meaningful G2 difference, primary ANCOVA with baseline G1, treatment-by-absence interaction, classroom-aware uncertainty and missing-data handling. First use pilot recruitment counts to ensure each primary stratum can support the precision target; do not select thresholds from outcome contrasts.

final_idea.title: Trigger temporary submeter logging after household load events
final_idea.question: With the same number of logged 10-minute intervals, does starting circuit-submeter logging immediately after a high aggregate Appliances interval capture more subsequent high-use intervals with a dominant measured circuit than week- and hour-matched random logging?
final_idea.new_claim: A two-stage monitoring policy may improve the yield of scarce circuit-level logging for characterizing persistent or recurring high-use episodes. This is a measurement-efficiency hypothesis, not a claim about reducing energy use.
final_idea.input_delta: The supplied data has whole-home Appliances Wh per completed 10-minute interval but no circuit readings. Add a prospective comparison of logging in the interval after an aggregate-load trigger versus equal-count, calendar-week and hour-of-day-matched random intervals, with synchronized circuit Wh evaluation labels.
final_idea.domain_value: A building-energy team could use limited temporary logger bandwidth to characterize circuits around recurring high-use episodes and prioritize later control or maintenance investigations.
assumptions: The whole-home meter reports each 10-minute interval soon enough to start circuit logging in the next interval.
Circuit meters can be synchronized to the whole-home meter, and measured circuit Wh can be reconciled with aggregate Appliances Wh within a pre-specified tolerance.
Some high-use episodes persist or recur into the following interval; this is unverified.
A single-home pilot can establish feasibility and within-home utility only, not generalization across households.
variables_and_units: Aggregate Appliances energy, Wh per completed 10-minute interval
Circuit-level energy, Wh per synchronized 10-minute interval
Logging effort, number of logged intervals

High-use capture yield, successful held-out intervals per 100 logging slots; success requires aggregate Appliances at or above the frozen threshold and a measured leading circuit contributing at least 50% of aggregate Appliances Wh
Calendar week and hour of day, matching strata
final_idea.testable_prediction: Set the event threshold to the 90th percentile of Appliances Wh in the first 60% of chronologically ordered rows, before examining held-out outcomes. In the held-out period, log the interval immediately after each threshold-crossing interval. At equal logging-slot count, week/hour-matched random schedules will have lower high-use capture yield than event-triggered schedules. The percentile, 50% circuit-share criterion, interval lag, and equal-budget rule are prospective choices; the computation returned here audits aggregate schedule feasibility only.
final_idea.alternative: High loads may be brief and end before the next interval; alternatively, circuits may share load and no single circuit may contribute half. In either case, event-triggered logging may have no higher circuit-attribution yield than matched random logging.
final_idea.discriminating_test: In a prospective single-home pilot, collect synchronized whole-home and circuit-level Wh continuously as reference truth during held-out evaluation, while scoring two pre-registered schedules with equal numbers of 10-minute slots: (a) log interval t+1 when Appliances at t meets or exceeds the 90th percentile frozen from the first 60% chronological calibration period, and (b) randomly choose the same number of slots matched within calendar week and hour of day. Define a successful slot as one where Appliances Wh is at or above the frozen threshold and the measured leading circuit contributes at least 50% of aggregate Appliances Wh. Compare successful slots per 100 logging slots; report paired week-level differences and uncertainty, retaining weeks with zero eligible slots. Continuous reference truth is needed to score unlogged counterfactual slots during this validation pilot, so it tests monitoring-policy value under reference instrumentation rather than immediate meter-cost savings.
final_idea.feasible_with_current_data: Partly. Dates and aggregate Appliances Wh support a calibration-only trigger, next-interval timing audit, and aggregate high-use capture comparison. The returned audit supports aggregate enrichment in this one chronological split. No circuit attribution, 50% share outcome, causal saving, or actual temporary-meter performance can be assessed.
final_idea.required_new_data: For an initial home pilot, obtain synchronized whole-home Appliances Wh and circuit-level Wh for every 10-minute interval during calibration and held-out weeks, with meter reconciliation and schedule activation/logging flags. Continuous circuit measurements serve as reference truth for this test. Replicate across homes before claiming household-level generalization or cost savings.
final_idea.failure_condition: The aggregate feasibility premise fails if the trigger yields too few held-out next-interval slots or does not enrich logged slots for above-threshold aggregate Wh compared with the matched random schedule. The circuit-level prediction fails if, at equal slot count, event-triggered logging does not increase successful slots per 100 over matched random logging, or if the gain is confined to isolated weeks. A single-home result cannot support a population claim.
final_idea.nearest_prior_query: Crossref query: residential household event-triggered circuit submeter logging compared with equal-budget, time-matched random logging for identifying circuits contributing to persistent or recurring high-load intervals.

original_final.what_changed: The interval trigger was corrected to start logging at t+1 after the completed aggregate interval t. The outcome now separates aggregate high-use capture from circuit attribution, fixes a 50% leading-circuit criterion and per-100-slot denominator, and specifies equal-count week/hour matching. The aggregate audit supports enrichment in this held-out split; the circuit-level claim remains untested. The literature search did not resolve novelty.
original_final.what_is_known: The supplied file has 19,735 ten-minute observations from one home over about 4.5 months, aggregate Appliances Wh and room/weather measurements, but no circuit labels, occupancy, or intervention records. The completed broker computation used 11,841 calibration rows and 7,894 held-out rows, froze q90 at 210 Wh, generated 697 next-interval trigger slots, and found 72.8838% above threshold versus a 22.9075% mean over 200 equal-count week/hour-matched random draws. This is descriptive aggregate schedule feasibility for one split and one home, not independent-household evidence or circuit attribution. Crossref returned eight relevance-ordered records, mostly titles/metadata; none directly establishes the proposed household circuit-submeter comparison, and the search scope is limited.
original_final.what_is_new_hypothesis: In a prospective pilot, using a prior-period q90 whole-home Appliances threshold to start circuit logging one interval later may yield more held-out high-use slots with a leading circuit contributing at least 50% of aggregate Appliances Wh per 100 logging slots than an equal-count week/hour-matched random schedule. This proposal adds a specific lagged monitoring policy, dominant-circuit outcome, and matched held-out comparison to the supplied information; world-literature novelty is undetermined.
original_final.falsifier: The aggregate feasibility premise is falsified if next-interval trigger slots are too sparse or are not enriched for above-threshold Appliances relative to matched random slots. The circuit-level hypothesis is falsified if the event-trigger schedule does not increase the registered successful-slot yield over matched random logging, or any increase disappears across held-out weeks.
original_final.minimum_next_test: Run a prospective single-home validation pilot with continuous synchronized whole-home Appliances Wh and per-circuit Wh at 10-minute resolution, using the first 60% chronologically only to freeze q90. On held-out weeks compare t+1 logging after threshold events with equal-count random slots matched by week and hour. Pre-register meter reconciliation tolerance, successful-slot definition (aggregate at/above q90 and leading circuit share at least 50%), per-100-slot yield, paired week-level uncertainty, and failure rule. Replicate homes before making population or cost-savings claims.
original_final.nearest_work_comparison: The supplied UCI documentation and listed Candanedo et al. 2017 paper concern regression prediction of aggregate appliance energy. The Crossref results include general event-triggered control or sampling titles, not a verified direct comparison of household circuit-submeter event schedules for dominant-circuit attribution. The search is limited and title-only in most records; it does not support a world-literature novelty claim.

World-literature novelty: undetermined; the limited Crossref search found no direct match but is not an exhaustive or full-text review.
original_final.limitations: Only aggregate Appliances Wh is available in the current dataset; no circuit attribution, intervention effect, energy saving, or household generalization can be inferred. The compute result is descriptive, tied to one chronological 60/40 split and one house, and the returned mean random yield has no reported uncertainty interval. Equal logged intervals proxy effort rather than full deployment cost. The Crossref index has limited coverage and mostly title/date/DOI metadata.

final_idea.title: Do post-entry wind-direction shifts precede sustained episode clearance?

assumptions: Retain episode entry at PM2.5 >=150 ug/m^3 immediately after an observed value below 150, and clearance as three consecutive observed hourly values below 75 ug/m^3 within six hours of entry; these are pilot definitions, not regulatory thresholds.

final_idea.title: Person-calibrated voice alerts for targeted clinical reassessment
final_idea.question: Can a sustained within-person shift in home voice features identify when an additional clinician assessment is more informative than waiting for the next scheduled visit?
final_idea.new_claim: Input delta: changes the objective from predicting interpolated UPDRS at each recording to deciding when to request an additional clinical measurement. The proposed contribution is a prespecified, person-calibrated persistent voice-deviation alert evaluated at a fixed alert burden against actual subsequent clinical assessment, not row-level predictive fit.
final_idea.domain_value: Could focus clinician time on periods when a patient's voice departs persistently from their own reference while limiting alerts for transient variability.
known_basis_refs: Supplied UCI 189 documentation: 5,875 repeated home recordings from 42 people over about six months; UPDRS targets are linearly interpolated.
assumptions: A prespecified initial reference period can estimate a useful personal voice baseline.
A sustained deviation sometimes precedes or accompanies clinically meaningful motor change, but may also arise from context, medication, illness, or ordinary variability.
An alert is actionable only if independent assessment can occur within the stated horizon.
final_idea.variables_and_units: Recording-level voice features in their supplied scales; elapsed time in days (test_time); baseline deviation as a dimensionless robust score per recording; trigger status per person-week; endpoint as actual clinician motor-UPDRS point change over the following 14 days; alert burden as alerts per person-month.
final_idea.testable_prediction: In prospective follow-up, at a fixed alert budget, person-weeks with a frozen persistent voice-deviation trigger will have a greater proportion of prespecified clinically meaningful motor-UPDRS changes within 14 days than matched non-trigger person-weeks with comparable assessment opportunity.
final_idea.alternative: Voice shifts mostly reflect recording context, vocal effort, medication timing, illness, or ordinary day-to-day variability and do not enrich for independently observed clinical change.
final_idea.discriminating_test: Before prospective outcome access, define an initial baseline window and a small voice-feature set using an independent calibration cohort; freeze robust within-person centers/scales and the trigger threshold there. Trigger when the prespecified deviation is exceeded on at least two consecutive scheduled recording days. Fix a maximum alert rate per person-month and a 14-day horizon. Compare trigger windows with within-person non-trigger windows matched on calendar period and opportunity for assessment. Primary endpoint: fraction followed by actual clinician motor-UPDRS change meeting a clinically meaningful threshold. Report paired enrichment, participant-level uncertainty, sensitivity, and alerts per person-month. Set the minimum useful enrichment margin before evaluation. This is a protocol proposal; no threshold is validated by the supplied data.
final_idea.feasible_with_current_data: Partly: exploratory trigger-rate and baseline/persistence sensitivity analyses are possible from the supplied repeated features and timestamps. The interpolated target series and absent raw visit dates/scores cannot establish trigger enrichment, independent lead time, or clinical utility.
final_idea.required_new_data: Prospective timestamped home recordings; exact dates and actual clinician motor-UPDRS scores at visits; clinically meaningful point-change and minimum enrichment thresholds defined before evaluation; an independent calibration cohort to freeze the feature set, baseline transformation, and trigger threshold; contemporaneous medication timing and brief illness/recording-context annotations. Unit: person-week trigger windows nested within participant, with assessment opportunity recorded.
final_idea.failure_condition: At the frozen alert budget, enrichment over matched non-trigger windows is below the prespecified minimum useful margin, or apparent enrichment vanishes when assessment opportunity and recorded context are considered.

final_idea.title: Replicate-aware voice change alerts
final_idea.question: For a remote-monitoring session, does averaging three standardized home voice recordings improve detection of clinically anchored within-person motor change compared with the first recording, at the same false-alert rate?
final_idea.new_claim: A replicate-based session estimate may separate short-term recording variability from persistent voice change enough to improve alert reliability. This is a proposal, not a finding in the supplied data.
final_idea.input_delta: Adds same-session repeats, a fixed aggregation rule, and a clinical alert comparison. Supplied rows lack replicate/session identifiers and a controlled repeat protocol.
final_idea.domain_value: Helps decide whether one voice capture is adequate or whether additional captures should be requested before acting on a change alert.
assumptions: Motor status is effectively unchanged during a replicate set collected minutes apart.
Prompt, microphone position, and recording procedure can be maintained at home.
The clinical comparison uses independently observed motor UPDRS assessments; interpolated labels are not independent clinical observations.
Clinicians prespecify the clinically meaningful score-change threshold, and alert cutoffs are selected using separate development participants before held-out evaluation.
final_idea.variables_and_units: Independent unit: participant, with sessions nested within participant. Collect three recordings minutes apart per session using the same task and setup; compare the first recording with the arithmetic mean of all three. Acoustic feature units are unspecified in the supplied documentation. Record follow-up time in days and independently observed clinician motor UPDRS in score points. Outcomes are within-session feature dispersion and held-out sensitivity for a prespecified clinically meaningful score change at a fixed false-alert rate.
final_idea.testable_prediction: In participant-held-out validation, the three-recording mean will have lower within-session acoustic dispersion and higher sensitivity for prespecified independently observed motor-UPDRS change than the first recording, at the same prespecified false-alert rate.
final_idea.alternative: Replicate differences mostly reflect real short-term symptom or medication-state fluctuation; averaging removes useful signal and does not improve or worsens detection of clinical change.
final_idea.discriminating_test: Collect three fixed-task recordings minutes apart at each home session, repeat sessions over follow-up, and obtain independently observed clinician motor-UPDRS assessments at prespecified visits. Prespecify the clinically meaningful score-change threshold with clinicians and fit the alert cutoff using separate development participants. In held-out participants compare the first recording with the three-recording mean at the same false-alert rate, with participant-level uncertainty. Record medication timing/state and setup conditions to assess alternative sources of within-session variation.
final_idea.feasible_with_current_data: Only a recording schedule-density check is feasible using subject# and test_time. No same-session repeatability, source attribution, or clinical alert validation is possible because replicate/session IDs and independent UPDRS labels at each recording are absent.
final_idea.required_new_data: Prospective sessions with three same-task recordings minutes apart, recording/session IDs, setup metadata, medication timing/state, repeated sessions per participant, and time-aligned independently observed clinician motor-UPDRS scores at clinical visits.
final_idea.failure_condition: The proposal is unsupported for this use if the mean fails to reduce within-session dispersion or improve held-out sensitivity at equal false-alert rate, or if any apparent benefit disappears under participant-held-out validation.
final_idea.nearest_prior_query: Crossref query for Parkinson home/remote voice studies directly comparing single recordings with same-session replicate aggregation for test-retest reliability or clinically anchored change alerts.

original_final.what_changed: The core candidate is retained but its protocol is revised: clinicians must define the meaningful score-change threshold, a separate participant development set must determine the alert cutoff, and final comparison is participant-held-out at an equal false-alert rate. No returned result establishes the proposed home voice replicate comparison.
original_final.what_is_new_hypothesis: Beyond the supplied benchmark framing, the study tests an operational measurement choice: whether averaging three standardized captures minutes apart improves clinically anchored motor-change alert sensitivity over the first capture at the same false-alert rate, and whether any gain coincides with lower within-session acoustic dispersion.
original_final.falsifier: The proposed use is unsupported if averaging three captures does not lower within-session dispersion or fails to improve held-out sensitivity at the same prespecified false-alert rate, or if the apparent gain disappears with participant-held-out validation.
original_final.minimum_next_test: Run a prospective pilot with three same-task home voice captures minutes apart per session, repeated sessions per participant, setup and medication timing/state metadata, and time-aligned independently observed clinician motor-UPDRS visits. Prespecify the meaningful score-change threshold, choose alert cutoffs in separate development participants, then compare first-capture and three-capture-mean alerts in held-out participants at equal false-alert rate with participant-level uncertainty. Use pilot repeatability and outcome variability to size a later confirmatory cohort.

final_idea.title: SCM share and project-specific strength qualification age
final_idea.question: For matched candidate formulations under a named project curing regime, does SCM replacement alter the age at which replicated batches meet a project-specified compressive-strength threshold, compared with a zero-SCM formulation at similar total binder and water-to-binder ratio?
final_idea.new_claim: Input increment: changes point-strength prediction into a concrete release/continue-curing decision evaluated over replicated batches and a predeclared threshold. Proposal-only causal hypothesis: under controlled, matched mix proportions and curing, larger slag-plus-fly-ash share may shift threshold attainment later while increasing later-age strength gain. The supplied rows descriptively support larger 7-to-28 and 28-to-56-day recipe-level gains for nonzero-SCM formulations, but do not test this controlled claim or the early-age prediction.
final_idea.domain_value: Could inform whether to release, continue curing, or reformulate a candidate mix when early strength matters.
known_basis_refs: UCI documentation: compressive strength is described as a nonlinear function of age and ingredients; age is in days and strength in MPa.

Yeh (1998), Modeling of strength of high-performance concrete using artificial neural networks, DOI 10.1016/S0008-8846(98)00165-3; listed as dataset introduction paper, without inferring a specific result.
assumptions: Repeated exact ingredient vectors can be compared as recipe-level observations, but are not known to be specimens from a shared batch.
SCM share is (slag + fly ash)/(cement + slag + fly ash); comparison requires overlap in total binder and water-to-binder ratio and is not randomized.
A project-specific strength threshold must be selected before a qualification study; the dataset supplies no universal threshold.
final_idea.variables_and_units: Cement, slag, fly ash, water, superplasticizer, coarse aggregate and fine aggregate in kg/m^3; age in days; strength in MPa. Derived covariates: SCM share (dimensionless), total binder (kg/m^3), water-to-binder ratio (dimensionless). Outcomes: within-recipe mean strength change (MPa) over prespecified age intervals and first observed threshold age (days).
final_idea.testable_prediction: Proposal-only, to be frozen for a new controlled study: at a prespecified threshold that both formulations eventually meet, the SCM formulation will reach it at a later sampled age and have greater 7-to-56-day gain than the matched zero-SCM formulation. The current table cannot test threshold age without a project threshold and cannot test 1-to-7-day SCM contrast because only two exact recipe pairs occur and both are zero-SCM.
final_idea.alternative: At matched total binder, water-to-binder ratio, aggregate proportions and curing, SCM share does not materially change threshold age or later interval gain; the current descriptive contrast reflects recipe selection or unrecorded batch/cure conditions.
final_idea.discriminating_test: Select a project threshold and practical difference before data collection. Cast replicated independent zero-SCM and SCM batches at matched total binder, water-to-binder ratio and aggregate proportions under the project curing regime; test specimens at 1, 7, 28 and 56 days. Compare batch-level mean strength gains over 7-to-56 days and first sampled threshold age, with uncertainty across independent batches. A practically negligible difference supports the alternative; a reproducible later threshold age with greater later gain supports the hypothesis.
final_idea.feasible_with_current_data: Partly: assess exact-recipe recurrence and descriptive recipe-level age contrasts. Cannot establish same-batch trajectories, causal substitution effects, curing effects, or qualification reliability.
final_idea.required_new_data: Mix/batch and specimen IDs; replicate specimens; controlled curing temperature and moisture history; documented proportions; strength test age and MPa; an application-specific threshold and release decision. Sample matched zero-SCM and SCM formulations at 1, 7, 28 and 56 days.
final_idea.failure_condition: The supplied-data early-age direction is not supported or testable: the only two exact 1-to-7-day recipe pairs are zero-SCM. The proposal is falsified for the defined mix/cure regime if replicated independent batches show neither a practically meaningful later 7-to-56-day gain nor a later threshold age under predeclared margins.
final_idea.nearest_prior_query: Crossref titles identify prior work explicitly on age-dependent strength development in slag concrete and blended cement, including temperature-matched curing and high-volume slag. A full-text review is needed to determine whether controlled matched threshold-age decisions remain open; no novelty is asserted.

original_final.what_changed: Retained I1 but narrowed it from a general SCM age-trajectory and threshold-age claim to a project-specific, batch-replicated qualification question. Executor correctly noted that the supplied table has no batch link or curing metadata and no universal threshold. Computation also showed that the frozen 1-to-7-day comparison has only two pairs, both zero-SCM, so that early-age contrast is not testable here. The 7-to-28 and 28-to-56 recipe-level contrasts point in the predicted later-gain direction, but remain descriptive. Search titles make broad age-dependent SCM strength development an established-neighbor area, so no broad novelty claim remains.

S1 returned eight relevance-ordered Crossref records, title/date/DOI only, with no abstracts and limited index coverage.
original_final.what_is_new_hypothesis: The case-input increment is an operational question: whether controlled SCM substitution changes a project-defined release age, alongside later strength gain, under a specified curing regime. This is proposal-only as a causal claim. The data offer descriptive later-age recipe contrasts in its predicted direction, not a mechanism or causal effect.
original_final.falsifier: In the defined controlled mix and curing regime, replicated independent batches show no practically meaningful increase in 7-to-56-day strength gain and no later attainment of the prespecified threshold for the SCM formulation, using margins declared before testing.
original_final.minimum_next_test: After choosing the project threshold and practical margins, prepare replicated independent batches of matched zero-SCM and SCM formulations with comparable total binder, water-to-binder ratio and aggregate proportions. Control curing; measure specimen compressive strength in MPa at 1, 7, 28 and 56 days, retaining batch and specimen IDs. Compare batch-level 7-to-56-day gains and first sampled threshold age under a predeclared rule.
original_final.nearest_work_comparison: The limited Crossref result set includes titles directly concerning compressive-strength development in blast-furnace-slag cement concrete under adiabatic and semi-temperature-matched curing (1998), prediction for Portland cement/blast-furnace-slag/fly-ash blends (1991), and strength development of concrete incorporating high-volume blast-furnace slag (1995). original_final.novelty_status: The idea adds to the supplied task by making project-specific threshold age and controlled batch replication the decision target. World-literature novelty is unverified; retrieved titles overlap strongly with age-dependent SCM strength development, and the search is limited to title-level Crossref results.
original_final.limitations: Exact ingredient recurrence does not verify common batches or curing histories. Age-pair availability is incomplete; the early pair cannot compare SCM groups, and the 28-to-56-day zero-SCM group has only three recipes. Recipe-level contrasts may reflect mixture selection and are not independent batch evidence. The search has limited coverage and title-only metadata.

final_idea.title: Batch-level calibration of 7-day strength for 28-day qualification
final_idea.question: In independently batched mixes designed for comparable 28-day strength and water/binder ratio, does the day-7/day-28 compressive-strength fraction differ between cement-only and SCM-containing binders, and does a pooled day-7 qualification cutoff produce binder-specific decision errors?
final_idea.new_claim: The input contributes a decision-linked, binder-family calibration question beyond single-row strength prediction. The supplied computation supports a lower early fraction for the specified SCM group descriptively; whether it generalizes to independent batches is a new hypothesis.
final_idea.domain_value: Determines whether a 7-day result can support a common early qualification rule or whether binder-specific calibration or later testing is needed.
assumptions: SCM share is (Blast Furnace Slag + Fly Ash)/(Cement + Blast Furnace Slag + Fly Ash).
Mixes can be designed in advance to comparable target 28-day strength and water/binder ranges; achieved 28-day strength is not used post hoc to define the experimental groups.
The dataset's exact-formulation records do not establish same-batch repeated specimens or shared curing history.

variables_and_units.experimental_unit: independent concrete batch, with specimen identifiers nested within batch
variables_and_units.age: day; primary measurements at 7 and 28 days
variables_and_units.SCM_share: dimensionless mass fraction of slag plus fly ash in total cementitious binder
variables_and_units.water_binder_ratio: dimensionless Water / (Cement + Blast Furnace Slag + Fly Ash)
variables_and_units.early_fraction: dimensionless batch-level day-7 mean strength / day-28 mean strength
variables_and_units.qualification_error: proportion of batches misclassified by a prespecified day-7 rule against the prespecified day-28 MPa requirement

final_idea.testable_prediction: In independently batched mixes planned to the same target 28-day strength and comparable water/binder ratio, the median batch-level early_fraction will be lower for the prespecified SCM-containing group (SCM share >0.30) than for cement-only mixes. The current table's overlap-restricted estimate is -0.1131 in median early_fraction (SCM minus cement), with formulation-resampled 95% interval [-0.1589, -0.0582].
final_idea.alternative: The independent-batch contrast is near zero or reverses; alternatively, a difference in early_fraction does not produce a practically important binder-specific qualification error under the agreed 28-day threshold.
final_idea.discriminating_test: Before testing, specify the 28-day qualification requirement in MPa, target-strength and water/binder matching tolerances, SCM definition, minimum practically important early_fraction difference, and acceptable false-pass/false-fail rates. Produce independent batches in both binder groups, randomly allocate replicate specimens from each batch to 7- and 28-day tests under recorded curing conditions, and compare batch-level early_fraction. Evaluate one pooled day-7 cutoff against the 28-day decision separately by binder group; compare it with a prespecified binder-specific rule. Report batch-level uncertainty and all exclusions.
final_idea.feasible_with_current_data: Only as an exploratory exact-formulation contrast. There are 114 exact-formulation pairs at ages 7 and 28; groups before overlap restriction are 45 cement-only and 49 SCM-share >0.30. Rectangular common support on day-28 strength and water/binder ratio retains 40 and 48 formulations. Batch identity, curing history and specimen replication are unavailable, so neither independence nor qualification error rates can be established.
final_idea.required_new_data: Independent batch and specimen identifiers; matched mix designs selected prospectively for comparable target 28-day strength and water/binder ratio; replicate compressive tests at days 7 and 28; curing temperature and moisture history; an application-defined 28-day strength requirement and acceptable classification-error rates.
final_idea.failure_condition: Revise away from a binder-specific early-strength rule if the independent-batch early_fraction contrast is practically negligible or opposite under the prespecified comparison, or if the pooled cutoff meets the agreed decision-error limits in both groups. Treat the current-data pattern as non-generalizing if independent batches do not reproduce it.
final_idea.nearest_prior_query: Compare with work on 7-to-28-day strength development and binder-specific qualification or threshold calibration at matched target strength and water/binder ratio; distinguish those decision tests from age-dependent strength formulas and generic prediction models.
final_idea.input_delta: Adds a falsifiable, operational question about whether early-strength qualification is calibrated across binder families, including a decision-error endpoint; this goes beyond the supplied generic composition-age-strength regression framing.

sources.title: Trait-specific testing of the equal environment assumption: The case of school grades and upper secondary school attendance
sources.original_abstract:
Objective: This paper tests the equal environment assumption for school grades and upper secondary school attendance and describes the conditions under which violations are problematic.
Background: A growing number of sociologists use twin-based research designs, particularly the Classical Twin Design (CTD), to differentiate between genetic and social causes of social inequalities. One key assumption of CTD is that environmental influences are shared by monozygotic and dizygotic twins to the same extent; called the equal environment assumption (EEA). This assumption is frequently contested and the target of concern, because violation can result in an overestimation of heritability and an underestimation of the role of the social environment.
Method: Using data from the first wave of the German TwinLife study, the paper illustrates two approaches to test EEA for school grades and enrolment in upper secondary school (Gymnasium). The analysis is based on a sample of twins (N = 1,576) aged ten to twelve years.
Results: The results show that the approaches are able to detect violations of EEA (though in different ways), depending on the environmental variables that might causally be involved in trait variance. Only in one case was a violation was observed; it had no effect on heritability estimates.
Conclusion: While EEA holds for school grades, violations do not automatically invalidate CTD in case of upper secondary school attendance.

sources.title: Residential electricity current and appliance dataset for AC-event detection from Indian dwellings
sources.original_abstract:
Abstract 
                   Air Conditioners (ACs) have become a major contributor to residential electricity consumption in India. Non-intrusive Load Monitoring (NILM) can be used to understand residential AC use and its contribution to electricity consumption. NILM techniques use ground truth information along with meter readings to train disaggregation algorithms. There are datasets available for disaggregation, but no dataset is available for a hot tropical country like India especially for AC event detection. Our dataset’s primary objective is to help train NILM algorithms for AC event detection and compressor operations. The dataset comprises of home-level electrical current consumption and manually tagged AC ground truth (ON/OFF status) data at 1-min interval, indoor environment temperature and relative humidity readings at 5-min interval and dwelling, AC and household characteristics. The data was collected from 11 homes located in a composite climate zone-Hyderabad, India for 19 summer days (May) 2019. The dataset consists of 1.6 million data points and 450 AC cycles with each cycle having a runtime of more than 60 min (> 2000 compressor ON/OF cycles). Public availability of such a dataset will allow researchers to develop, train and test NILM algorithms that recognize AC and identify compressor operations.

sources.title: Mapping exposure to particulate pollution during severe haze episode using improved MODIS AOT‐PM<sub>10</sub> regression model with synoptic meteorology classification
sources.original_abstract: Abstract  Severe smoke haze from biomass burning is frequently observed in Northern Thailand during dry months of February–April. Sparsely located monitoring stations operated in this vast mountainous region could not provide sufficient particulate matter (PM) data for exposure risk assessment. Satellite aerosol optical thickness (AOT) data could be used, but their reliable relationship with ground‐based PM data should be first established. This study aimed to improve the regression model between PM 10  and Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer AOT with consideration of synoptic patterns to better assess the exposure risk in the area. Among four synoptic patterns, each representing the totality of meteorology governing Northern Thailand on a given day, most severe haze days belonged to pattern 2 that featured conditions of clear sky, stagnant air, and high PM 10  levels. AOT‐24 h PM 10  regression model for pattern 2 had coefficient of determination improved to 0.51 from 0.39 of combined case. Daily exposure maps to PM 10  in most severe haze period of February–April 2007 were produced for Chiangmai, the largest and most populated province in Northern Thailand. Regression model for pattern 2 was used to convert 24 h PM 10  ranges of modified risk scale to corresponding AOT ranges, and the mapping was done using spatially continuous AOT values. The highest exposure risk to PM 10  was shown in urban populated areas. Larger numbers of forest fire hot spots and more calm winds were observed on the days of higher exposure risk. Early warning and adequate health care plan are necessary to reduce exposure risk to future haze episodes in the area.

sources.title: Drivers of the 2016 particulate matter pollution episode &#160;over northern India
sources.original_abstract: Intense episodes of fine particulate matter (PM2.5) pollution often overwhelm large areas of the  Indo-Gangetic Plain (IGP) in northern India during the post-monsoon season, a time when crop residue burning is at its peak. We conduct idealised emission sensitivity experiments using the WRF-Chem model to investigate the leading causes and spatiotemporal extent of one such extreme episode from 31 0ct - 8 Nov 2016, when hourly PM2.5 levels exceeded 500 µg m–3across much of the IGP on several days. We utilise the anthropogenic emissions from EDGARv5.0 and the latest FINNv2.5 for fire emissions and evaluate modelled and observed ambient PM2.5 and black carbon  (BC) concentrations across the IGP. The model captured the PM2.5 and BC peaks during the latter half of the episode and underestimated on other days. We find that biomass burning (BB) emissions during this episode have the strongest effect across the source regions in the upper (NW) IGP, followed by Delhi (middle IGP), where it contributes 50 - 80 % to 24-h mean PM2.5. Complete elimination of BB emissions decreases PM2.5 concentrations by 400 µg m–3  (80 - 90 %) in the upper IGP and by 280 µg m–3  (40 - 80 %) across the middle IGP during this episode. Contributions from the BB source to daily varying BC concentrations are 80-90 %, 40 - 85 % and 10 - 60 % across upper, middle and lower IGP, respectively. BB emissions dominantly contribute to daily mean secondary organic aerosols (80 %), primary organic aerosols (90 %), dust (60 %), and nitrate (50 %) components of PM2.5 across the upper and middle IGP. In comparison, the anthropogenic share of these compounds was nearly one-third everywhere except across the lower IGP. The buildup of the episode across the middle IGP was facilitated by prolonged atmospheric stratification and stagnation, causing BB-derived BC and PM2.5 to be trapped in the lowest 1 km. Our work emphasises the need for rigorous policy interventions during post-monsoon to reduce agricultural crop burning, together with targeted anthropogenic emissions control across the IGP, to minimise such extreme episodes in the future.

sources.title: Dam safety assessment through data-level anomaly detection and information fusion
sources.original_abstract: The anomaly detection and safety assessment of dams have attracted increasing attentions. To assess the safety of dams, a novel dam safety assessment model is proposed. The safety assessment model consists of data-level anomaly detection and information fusion. In the anomaly detection, a novel model based on the generative adversarial network and variational autoencoder is proposed. Through the stepwise training, the anomaly scores with reconstruction and discrimination losses can be obtained. Considering the multi-source and complexity of information system, a two-step fusion model is proposed. In the multi-source and multi-attribute fusion, the neighborhood rough set model is employed to construct the neighborhood granular structure. Through the idea of granular computing, the uncertainty of these sources and attributes is measured. Then the Sup-Inf fusion functions and fusion weights are employed to integrate the information. Finally, the anomaly scores with interval form are obtained. For verification, an arch dam is taken as an example. Through the analysis of detection and fusion results, the proposed model can detect the abnormal signals accurately and have the comprehensive assessment of the dam.

sources.title: A Hybrid Multi-Model Framework for Personalized User-Level Anomaly Detection With Data-Driven Threshold Optimization
sources.original_abstract: Modern user authentication systems increasingly need user and device behavior aware adaptive mechanism to detect evolving threats beyond the traditional authentication framework of static credential verification. This paper proposes a hybrid multi-model framework for personalized user-level anomaly detection using a data-driven Hybrid Anomaly Score (HAS). Unlike static thresholding approaches, The proposed framework derives algorithm that integrates multiple anomaly detection methodologies to compute HAS through adaptive per-user thresholds (using cohort maturity and percentile-based optimization). The framework is evaluated on 72 million real-world data set. The framework demonstrate 96% precision, 92% recall, and an F1-score of 0.94, while maintaining inference latency within 2-3 ms per authentication event. The ablation analysis of the framework confirms the contribution of dynamic weighting and personalized threshold optimization to improved detection stability and convergence. The proposed framework outperforms existing approaches in both scalability and latency satisfying real-time operational constraint. The results indicate that data-driven adaptive thresholding combined with hybrid anomaly modeling provides an effective and deployable solution for large-scale authentication environments.

sources.title: A rapid pupillometry protocol for clinical use: Effect of age and test-retest repeatability
sources.original_abstract:
Abstract 
                 
                   Purpose: 
                  Pupillometry is most commonly performed in laboratory settings using specialized, non-portable instruments that require lengthy test protocols. The purpose of this study was to develop and evaluate a rapid, clinically-applicable pupillometry protocol using a commercially available, portable, handheld instrument.
                   Methods: 
                  Thirty-seven healthy individuals (ages 21- 61 years) participated in three experiments. In each experiment, the pupillary light reflex (PLR) was elicited by full-field, 500-ms chromatic flashes (470 nm and 621 nm; 12,000 Td). Experiment I evaluated the minimum dark adaptation (DA) time needed to achieve maximum PLRs. Experiment II determined the effect of age. Experiment III estimated PLR test-retest repeatability. For all experiments, baseline pupil size (BL; 1 sec before flash onset), maximum pupil constriction (MPC) following the flash, and post-illumination pupillary response (PIPR; median size 6 - 8 sec after flash offset) were quantified.
                   Results: 
                  Experiment I showed that from 1 - 3 min of DA, BL and MPC increased slightly (0.27 mm and 5%, respectively), whereas the PIPR increased considerably (17%). The responses did not change appreciably after 3 min, therefore a 3-min DA period was used for Experiments II and III. Experiment II showed a trend for BL and MPC to decrease with age, but correlations with age were not statistically significant (all p > 0.05). PIPR was independent of age (r = -0.01; p = 0.96). Experiment III showed test-retest repeatability of approximately 1 mm for BL, and 10% for MPC and PIPR, indicating good repeatability.
                   Conclusion: 
                  The proposed approach is useful for measuring the MPC and PIPR across a broad range of ages and baseline pupil sizes. Given the device portability and short test duration (approximately 5 minutes including DA), this approach has promising clinical utility.

sources.title: An Augmentation of Abrams’ Law: Correlate Compressive Strength with Water-binder Ratio of Concrete Containing Fly Ash
sources.original_abstract:
Introduction/Objective 
                     The study presents an augmented form of Abrams’ law that describes the relationship between the strength and water-binder ratio of concrete. This augmentation permits the prediction of the compressive strength of concrete containing fly ash regardless of the mass substitutions of cement by fly ash and the testing age within the ranges of 14-120 days. 
                   
                   
                     Methods 
                     In the modified Abrams’ law, the (apparent) water-binder ratio is replaced by the effective one in which the reactivity of fly ash is considered, and the substitution ratio of fly ash is included. The empirical parameters in the augmented formula have been determined with multi-linear regression analysis based on experimental data. 
                   
                   
                     Results 
                     The goodness of the curve fitting to this renewed strength formula is excellent. The compressive strength predicted from the augmentation coincides with its measured counterpart in the literature. 
                   
                   
                     Discussion 
                     Abrams’ law is augmented by introducing effective water-binder ratio and fly ash replacement rate, and verifies it through regression analysis of experimental and literature data. This topic has practical significance and contributes to the mixture design of sustainable concrete. 
                   
                   
                     Conclusion 
                     The Abrams’ formula is basically simple but has restricted limits of validity. The proposed augmentation improves the accuracy of the strength estimation of sustainable concrete mixtures batched with mineral admixtures such as fly ash.

sources.title: XGBoost-Based Prediction of the 28-Day Compressive Strength of Portland Cement Concrete Containing Blast Furnace Slag and Fly Ash
sources.original_abstract: Reducing Portland Cement (PC) consumption through Fly Ash (FA) and Blast Furnace Slag (BFS) can lower concrete’s environmental burden, but the coupled effects of these constituents make 28-day compressive strength difficult to estimate with conventional empirical relationships. Accordingly, this study developed an interpretable Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost)-based model for predicting the 28-day compressive strength of high-performance Portland cement concrete incorporating these supplementary cementitious materials. For this purpose, a database comprising 415 normally cured mixtures tested at 28 days was adopted. Eight predictors were considered: theoretical mixture density and the gravimetric proportions of PC, FA, BFS, water, superplasticizer, coarse aggregate, and fine aggregate. The predictive performance was assessed using shuffled six-fold cross-validation. Meanwhile, pooled out-of-fold predictions achieved a coefficient of determination (R2) of 0.85, a mean absolute error of 3.55 MPa, and a root mean squared error of 5.62 MPa. In addition, fold-specific R2 values ranged from 0.80 to 0.90. Native XGBoost importance and SHapley Additive exPlanations ranked PC content, water content, and theoretical density as the leading input variables in terms of predictive significance. In this way, the proposed XGBoost model can support preliminary strength estimation and screening of eco-friendly mix designs before laboratory verification. Regardless, its use should remain within the represented compositional ranges until independent validation confirms transferability.

sources.title: Global Assessment of Urban Bike-Sharing Sensitivity and Resilience to Extreme Weather
sources.original_abstract: As climate extremes intensify, assessing how bike-sharing systems respond and recover is vital for urban resilience. This study develops a comparative framework using a time-series Transformer model and scenario analysis to evaluate demand under extreme heat, cold, heavy rain, and snowfall, using hourly trip and weather data from 14 cities worldwide (2023–2025). The sensitivity analysis shows that extreme heat reduces demand by over 40% in hotter cities but remains stable in temperate ones, while extreme cold and snowfall cause the strongest suppression, often exceeding 80%. To capture resilience, we simulate recovery curves after rainfall and snowfall shocks: North American systems typically rebound within 6–7 hours, whereas Montreal and Seoul show more prolonged disruptions, while Oslo and New York recover faster with winter operations and flatter demand profiles. These findings highlight how climatic exposure and operational readiness shape resilience and provide evidence to support climate-adaptive management and long-term system planning.

sources.title: Probabilistic Bike-Sharing Demand Forecasting under Changing Weather and Seasonal Regimes with Transformer-Based Models
sources.original_abstract: Bike-sharing systems must plan fleet and rebalancing under changing weather and seasonal regimes. We conduct reproducible probabilistic one-hour-ahead demand forecasting on two public datasets (UCI Bike Sharing hourly data and Seoul Bike Sharing Demand) under forward-chaining temporal splits. We compare tree-based Random Forest and XGBoost quantile baselines with N-BEATS, a Transformer encoder, an Informer-lite encoder, and a Temporal Fusion Transformer (TFT). Across both cities, N-BEATS and tree models yield the lowest MAE, while TFT produces the best calibrated 80% prediction intervals (81.1% coverage in Seoul). Error and coverage degrade under extreme weather, motivating uncertainty-aware operations.

sources.title: Explaining Station-Level Weather Sensitivity in Bike-Sharing Systems: A Spatial Analysis of Chicago's Divvy Network
sources.original_abstract: Weather conditions are widely recognized as important determinants of bike-sharing demand. However, existing research has primarily focused on estimating average weather effects at the system, city, or user-group level, providing limited insight into why some stations are substantially more weather-sensitive than others. This study develops and applies a station-level Weather Sensitivity Index (WSI) to examine the spatial, built-environment, and socioeconomic determinants of weather sensitivity within Chicago’s Divvy bike-sharing system. The analysis proceeds in three stages. First, station-specific weather-response functions are estimated using three years of daily bike-sharing data and Negative Binomial regression models. Second, station-level responses to temperature, precipitation, snowfall, and wind are transformed into four dimensions of weather sensitivity and combined through Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to construct a composite WSI. Third, Ordinary Least Squares (OLS), Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), and spatial econometric models are employed to identify the factors associated with variation in weather sensitivity across stations. The results reveal substantial heterogeneity in station-level weather responses. Highly weather-sensitive stations are concentrated along Chicago’s lakefront and within recreational, tourism-oriented, and destination-focused environments, whereas stations located in more residential and activity-rich areas exhibit greater demand stability. Built-environment and socioeconomic characteristics explain a substantial share of observed variation in weather sensitivity. Stations located closer to Lake Michigan and within highly connected street networks tend to exhibit greater weather sensitivity, whereas higher activity density, larger shares of low-wage workers, and higher proportions of households owning multiple vehicles are associated with lower weather sensitivity. Spatial diagnostics reveal strong spatial clustering and significant spillover effects, indicating that weather sensitivity is influenced not only by local station characteristics but also by neighboring stations. The study contributes to the literature by shifting attention from average weather effects to variation in weather sensitivity, introducing a composite WSI, and demonstrating the importance of spatial processes in shaping weather-related vulnerability within urban bike-sharing systems. The findings provide practical guidance for targeted resilience planning and weather-responsive management of shared micromobility networks.

sources.title: Global Assessment of Urban Bike-Sharing Sensitivity and Resilience to Extreme Weather
sources.original_abstract: As climate extremes intensify, assessing how bike-sharing systems respond and recover is vital for urban resilience. This study develops a comparative framework using a time-series Transformer model and scenario analysis to evaluate demand under extreme heat, cold, heavy rain, and snowfall, using hourly trip and weather data from 14 cities worldwide (2023–2025). The sensitivity analysis shows that extreme heat reduces demand by over 40% in hotter cities but remains stable in temperate ones, while extreme cold and snowfall cause the strongest suppression, often exceeding 80%. To capture resilience, we simulate recovery curves after rainfall and snowfall shocks: North American systems typically rebound within 6–7 hours, whereas Montreal and Seoul show more prolonged disruptions, while Oslo and New York recover faster with winter operations and flatter demand profiles. These findings highlight how climatic exposure and operational readiness shape resilience and provide evidence to support climate-adaptive management and long-term system planning.

sources.title: Exploring the Weather Impact on Bike Sharing Usage Through a Clustering Analysis
sources.original_abstract: Bike sharing systems (BSS) have been a popular traveling service for years and are used worldwide. It is attractive for cities and users who wants to promote healthier lifestyles; to reduce air pollution and greenhouse gas emission as well as improve traffic. One major challenge to docked bike sharing system is redistributing bikes and balancing dock stations. Some studies propose models that can help forecasting bike usage; strategies for rebalancing bike distribution; establish patterns or how to identify patterns. Other studies propose to extend the approach by including weather data. This study aims to extend upon these proposals and opportunities to explore how and in what magnitude weather impacts bike usage. Bike usage data and weather data are gathered for the city of Washington D.C. and are analyzed using k-means clustering algorithm. K-means managed to identify three clusters that correspond to bike usage depending on weather conditions. The results show that the weather impact on bike usage was noticeable between clusters. It showed that temperature followed by precipitation weighted the most, out of five weather variables.
